newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq assembly approves initial oil deal with China.
newsitem.headline: Iraq assembly approves initial oil deal with China.

text.p: Iraq's National Assembly has approved an initial oil deal with China to develop an Iraqi oilfield, the official Iraqi newspapers said on Sunday.

The papers, quoting the head of parliament's oil and energy committe Munther al-Alousi, said the deal would be signed soon to develop al-Ahdab oilfield near the city of Kut 170 km (100 miles) south of Baghdad.
The official Chinese news agency Xinhua said last week that Iraq and China were discussing a plan to help develop an oilfield with annual capacity of 15 million tonnes.

The Iraqi papers said it was a 26-year investment plan. Four years would be devoted for constructing the field and the rest was to handle oil production before the whole project would be handed to the Iraqi government.
The papers said: "(Chinese) companies are committed to implement the project soon after signing it and under the unjust (U.N.) trade sanctions."
The sanctions, imposed after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, include a ban in Baghdad's oil exports and imports of all commodities except for essentials.

Iraq and the United Nations reached in May an agreement allowing Baghdad limited oil sales worth $2 billion in renewable six months time. The deal stalled since September when Baghdad sent troops to help one Kurdish faction fight a rival.
"The positive aspact of the contract...is that it represents a step toward breaking the embargo," Alousi said.
China, a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council, supports easing or lifting the sanctions.
Last August, Baghdad signed with Beijing an agreement to boost their trade once the oil-for-food deal is settled.
